job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Sara Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm on my laptop at the table in the room I share with Ruth, a friend from church, in a flat in Brookhaven. I use an AI assistant to draft my applications and to check my spreadsheets, and I've started a small thing on the side: I do payroll and tax paperwork for three family guesthouses, which my parents' guesthouse in Linden Falls introduced me to. Evenings I work the front desk at a hotel, four nights a week, which pays the rent. I studied business and accounting at Hartfield University, top of the year, with internships in a hotel group's finance office and at a family furniture maker. Five months out, 43,000 of debt, no offer yet, and my parents can't help because their season's been thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's good news for ordinary people, because it means the economy carries on and small firms keep going. I'd tell my friends that what matters is working hard and being honest. I'd also say don't let anyone sell you a miracle, either a good one or a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still anxious, because the money's tight. I owe 43,000, I work four nights at the desk and my savings wouldn't cover a month. The AI plateau doesn't make a finance job appear in Brookhaven, and I'm tired of hearing that things will sort themselves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the three guesthouses and aim for eight by the end of next year, since small hotels have no accountant and need one. I'd keep the front desk nights and apply for roles in hospitality finance, where my internship counts. I'd also ask the hotel group's finance manager for a reference, which she offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired but stubborn. I pray in the mornings, and I keep a list of small wins so the days don't blur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you land the three guesthouses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum told one of her guests, who owns a farm stay, and the guest told two others. It's word of mouth, which is how my family has always found work. Nobody asked for a degree, they asked whether I'd be honest and on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your faith say to you about this period?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells me to work, to be patient and to trust that things come in their own time. I don't think waiting means being passive, though, so I work as hard as I can and leave the rest. I find that steadies me.

say: The economy carries on and small firms keep going, so what matters is **honest work**.
Don't let anyone sell you a **miracle**, good or bad.
think: I'm still anxious: **43,000** owed and savings that wouldn't cover a month.
A plateau doesn't make a finance job appear in **Brookhaven**.
do: Keep the three guesthouses and aim for **eight** by the end of next year.
Keep the front desk **nights** and apply for hospitality finance roles.
Ask the hotel group's finance manager for a **reference**.
feel: **Tired** but stubborn, with prayer and a list of small wins.
S0.quote: Nobody asked for a degree, they asked whether I'd be honest and on time.
fieldNote: Work comes through **word of mouth** and church-type networks, a pattern she trusts.
Money is the pressure: **debt**, four night shifts and a thin cushion.
Her faith is **active**: waiting doesn't mean being passive.

steps.text: Grow the guesthouse payroll clients from three to eight
Apply for finance roles in hotel groups and hospitality
Keep four front desk night shifts a week
Ask the hotel group's finance manager for a reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great chance for people who work, and a hard time for those who don't adapt. I'd tell friends to use it for the boring work and to keep the human touch for the clients. And I'd say the answer is training and enterprise, not waiting for the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit unsettled. Hotel group finance offices cut their junior teams first, because the work is routine. Where I interned, three of the eight clerks left and weren't replaced, so the ladder I wanted to climb is shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my side business into a proper small firm, with a name, a simple contract and a price list. I'd offer a package: payroll, tax and a monthly chat about the numbers, since the chat is what people value. I'd also take a short course in hospitality tax rules, so I know more than the software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mixed with a bit of nerves. It feels as though the change has finally come to my door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does it do for your guesthouse clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tidies the payroll, flags errors, and writes the first draft of the monthly summary. I check it all before it goes, and I spend my time on the conversation with the owner. That's the part they pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about clients just buying the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will, and they'll be fine with it. The ones who value a person will stay, particularly the older owners who want somebody they know. I'd rather build on the people who value a person, since that's the market that won't vanish.

say: It's a great chance for people who work, and a hard time for those who don't **adapt**.
The answer is **training and enterprise**, not waiting for the state.
think: Hotel finance offices cut juniors first, and three of eight clerks left and weren't **replaced**.
The ladder I wanted to climb is **shorter**.
do: Turn the side business into a small **firm** with a name, a contract and a price list.
Offer a **package** of payroll, tax and a monthly chat about the numbers.
Take a short course in **hospitality tax** rules.
feel: **Excited**, with nerves: change has finally come to my door.
S1.quote: The ones who value a person will stay, particularly the older owners who want somebody they know.
fieldNote: Sees the threat but turns it into a **business** model: people-first small firms.
Wants **enterprise** over state help, in line with her free-market views.
Her edge is **real**: daily tool use plus clients she already has.

steps.text: Register a small payroll and tax firm with a simple contract
Sell a package of payroll, tax and monthly check-ins
Take a short course in hospitality tax rules
Automate payroll drafts with an AI assistant and check each one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd need to pull together as families and as communities, and that nobody can wait for a rescue. I'd say it at church and at the hotel. I'd tell people to cut debts, keep jobs and help their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be frightened. My side business does thinking work, so it faces the same machine as the jobs I'm applying for. I'd probably have a year where I'm more useful than most and then a cliff. And my debt wouldn't care about any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on two things. I'd grow the guesthouse clients as far as I can and bring in as much cash as possible, and I'd learn something hands-on, like running a small guesthouse myself, since my parents are in that trade and robots take longer there. I'd put every spare cent at the loan and sell anything that isn't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and awake at night. But I keep reminding myself that I have a family, a church and a trade, and many people have less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would happen to the guesthouses you serve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guesthouses would likely still need hosts, cleaning and cooking, which robots take longer to do. But their paperwork would be done by software, so I'd lose that. I'd help them move towards what only a person can do, like welcoming people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for help from anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From family and church, yes, without hesitation. From the state, only for something like a training place or a short loan pause. I'd rather build than wait for a cheque.

say: We need to pull together as **families** and communities, and nobody can wait for a rescue.
Cut debts, keep jobs and help your **neighbours**.
think: My side business does thinking work, so it faces the same **machine** as the jobs I'm applying for.
I'd have maybe a year of being useful and then a **cliff**.
do: Grow the guesthouse clients and bring in as much **cash** as I can.
Learn to run a small **guesthouse** myself, since robots reach it later.
Put every spare cent at the **loan** and sell what I don't need.
feel: **Scared** and awake at night, but grateful for family, church and a trade.
S2.quote: I'd rather build than wait for a cheque.
fieldNote: Falls back on her **parents'** trade, a hands-on field with a three-year gap.
Accepts help from family and church but wants the state's aid kept **short** and tied to training.
Fear is real but her **action** list is long, which keeps her anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Sign up as many guesthouse payroll clients as I can handle
Learn guesthouse running from my parents in Linden Falls
Put every spare cent at the student loan
Ask the church for work leads and a spare room if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is time for people who start now, and the ones who wait will be sorry. I'd tell friends to build something small that serves real people. I'd stay positive in public, because fear spreads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good about it. I have the clients, the habit of using the tools and five years to build something that can stand without me doing every task. If I can have twenty clients by 2029, I'd have a business that survives most of what comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the firm, grow to eight guesthouses next year and then to twenty. I'd bring in a part-timer, probably Ruth, and teach her the system. I'd pay 500 a month at the loan and put the same amount into a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with healthy nerves. The window feels wide enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What changes in how you grow the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change from selling hours to selling a service. A monthly fee covers payroll, tax and advice, and I use the tools to deliver it. That makes it a business and not just a freelance job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hire, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, who's reliable and good with people, though not a numbers person. I'd rather hire for character and teach the skills, since the tools do a lot of the number work now.

say: Five years is time for people who start **now**, and the ones who wait will be sorry.
Build something small that serves **real people**.
think: I have the clients, the tool habit and five years to build something that stands without me doing every **task**.
Twenty clients by 2029 would **survive** most of what comes.
do: Register the firm, reach **eight** guesthouses next year and then twenty.
Hire **Ruth** part-time and teach her the system.
Pay **500** a month at the loan and save the same amount.
feel: **Optimistic**, with healthy nerves: the window feels wide enough to build.
S3.quote: I'd rather hire for character and teach the skills, since the tools do a lot of the number work now.
fieldNote: Time lets her move from **freelancing** to a service with a monthly fee.
Would hire her friend Ruth, so loyalty and **character** guide her.
Debt remains but she has a **path** to clear it.

steps.text: Register the firm and grow to eight guesthouse clients next year
Hire Ruth part-time and teach her the payroll system
Pay 500 a month at the student loan and save the same

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot, and it should be a hopeful time for those who work. I'd tell people to use the years to build something, and I'd say that the church and the community have a role in looking after people. I'd keep it upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel good about it. I could grow my firm, clear the loan and still have time to marry and start a family. If the thinking work does get taken over by 2036, I'd have a business that rests on trust, which is harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the firm to a steady twenty or thirty clients, take a part-time partner, and clear the debt in about five years. I'd keep learning every new tool because they get better each year. I'd save for a deposit on a small place, and put some money into a sensible fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, and glad. I'd probably say a prayer of thanks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Where do you see the guesthouse trade and yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the guesthouse trade survives, because people like to be welcomed by someone. The paperwork side goes to software, so I'd be serving them on the advice and the human side. And I'd like to run a small guesthouse of my own one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum and dad to start learning the tools now, with me beside them, so they can use them for bookings and tax. I'd say we can help each other as a family firm, and that they should retire when they're ready, not when they're pushed.

say: Ten years is a lot, and it should be a **hopeful** time for those who work.
Church and community have a role in **looking after** people.
think: I could grow my firm, clear the loan and still have time to **marry** and start a family.
A business built on **trust** is harder to replace.
do: Grow the firm to **twenty or thirty** clients and clear the debt in about five years.
Keep learning every new **tool** as it arrives.
Save a **deposit** for a small place and invest in a sensible fund.
feel: **Settled** and glad, probably with a prayer of thanks.
S4.quote: I'd tell my mum and dad to start learning the tools now, with me beside them, so they can use them for bookings and tax.
fieldNote: Her **trust**-based business gives her real security in the long run.
Looks after her **parents'** guesthouse as well as her own plans.
Family firm and faith are **linked** in her picture of a good life.

steps.text: Grow the firm to twenty or thirty clients

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because I need time to build the firm and the clients before the thinking work goes, and two years isn't enough with this debt. What would help is a loan pause, small-business support for people starting out and word of mouth from people who trust me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that young people aren't helpless. We're willing to work nights, start small and learn the tools. We'd just like someone to see that we're trying and give us a fair go.

headlineQuote: Young people aren't helpless. We're willing to work nights, start small and learn the tools.
portrait: Sara is 23, top of her business and accounting class, working **front desk nights** and sharing a room with her friend Ruth.
She owes 43,000, runs payroll for three family guesthouses and uses AI tools every day.
She is traditional, churchgoing and pro-enterprise, and prefers to **build** rather than wait for the state.
Her mood lifts as time grows, because trust-based small-firm work suits a longer runway.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because two years is too short to build clients before thinking work goes.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan pause**, small-business support for people starting out and local word-of-mouth referrals.
